authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review covers tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution, a technique in nanoscale optical imaging.
motivation: The paper aims to summarize recent advances in tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy, which combines scanning probe techniques with optical fluorescence to achieve superresolution beyond the diffraction limit.
method: The review discusses the principles of using a scanning tip as a nanoscale optical antenna to confine electromagnetic fields, and surveys experimental techniques and insights from molecular fluorescence studies.
result: The review highlights that tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy can achieve atomic-scale spatial resolution, enabling the study of electronic and vibronic properties of individual molecules and submolecular structures.
conclusion: The technique offers a powerful tool for nanoscale imaging and spectroscopy, with potential applications in materials science and molecular identification.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This review paper discusses the fundamental physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the mechanisms of arcing and its impact on accelerator technology.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices, so understanding its fundamental mechanisms is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The paper synthesizes recent experimental and simulation results to present a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown, involving surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles.
result: The review provides a unified understanding of the complex interactions that trigger vacuum breakdown, offering insights for improving high-power technologies.
conclusion: Advances in experiments and simulations have led to a coherent mechanistic picture of vacuum breakdown, which can guide the development of more reliable and efficient accelerators.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications, including magnetism, topology, and spintronics.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D van der Waals magnets, which have challenged established theories and opened new applications.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes experimental and theoretical results on 2D magnets, covering topics such as ferromagnetism, antiferromagnetism, topology, magnons, and interactions with light and electric fields.
result: The review highlights new phenomena and expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental techniques in 2D magnetism.
conclusion: The field of 2D van der Waals magnets is actively evolving, with potential for future applications in spintronics and other areas.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review unifies the theory of radiation forces and torques in optical and acoustic fields, focusing on their applications in particle manipulation.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a comprehensive overview of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in wave fields induce forces and torques on particles, a topic with broad applications in trapping and sorting.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes existing theoretical and experimental results, presenting a unified perspective across optics and acoustics.
result: It discusses applications such as optical trapping, acoustic sorting, and pulling forces, highlighting the common underlying physics.
conclusion: The review consolidates knowledge on radiation forces and torques, offering a unified framework that may inspire future research in wave-matter interactions.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review on space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics, focusing on brickwork quantum circuits.
motivation: To provide a unified view of quantum many-body dynamics via space-time duality, drawing analogies with quantum computation.
method: Review of theoretical concepts and results on space-time duality in lattice systems, emphasizing brickwork quantum circuits.
result: Presents a framework for understanding exactly solvable dynamics in interacting many-body systems.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful perspective for studying quantum dynamics, with connections to quantum computation.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars with future detectors and emphasizes multimessenger observations.
motivation: The paper aims to highlight the scientific potential of continuous gravitational wave searches and their connection to electromagnetic astronomy and nuclear astrophysics.
method: It is a review article that surveys detection prospects, detector capabilities, and the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: The paper discusses the expected sensitivity of future detectors and the implications for understanding dense matter and neutron star physics.
conclusion: Multimessenger observations with continuous gravitational waves could provide unique insights into neutron star interiors and astrophysical processes.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from lattice geometry and correlations.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals.
result: It highlights the role of frustration, spin-orbit coupling, and interference effects in generating novel electronic states.
conclusion: Kagome metals serve as a platform for exploring strongly correlated topological physics, but the work is primarily a materials science review without direct quantum information or thermodynamics focus.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, unifying approaches for complex systems.
motivation: To provide a unified framework for modeling diverse stochastic reaction-diffusion systems in physics, chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
method: The authors review and apply field-theoretic techniques, including path integrals and quantum field theory methods, to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.
result: The review demonstrates how these methods unify various approaches and can be applied to a wide range of complex systems.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods offer a powerful and unifying framework for studying stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, with broad applicability.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes how gravitational-wave and X-ray observations of neutron stars constrain the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe, and their properties provide crucial information about the behavior of matter under extreme compression.
method: The paper reviews recent observational results from gravitational-wave signals of binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, and compares them to theoretical predictions from nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: The measurements constrain neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, which are used to test and refine the nuclear equation of state at high densities.
conclusion: The review provides an outlook on future observational opportunities that will further constrain the dense matter equation of state.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiments, theory, and simulations, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research, emphasizing the synergy between experimental, theoretical, and computational approaches.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes findings from experiments, theoretical models, and large-scale simulations in spin-glass systems.
result: The review tracks progress in understanding spin-glass dynamics and highlights future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass research benefits from interdisciplinary collaboration, and the field continues to offer open questions.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are exotic states of matter with potential applications in quantum computing, but their realization is challenging.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev model) and experimental progress in candidate materials.
result: Summarizes key properties such as chiral edge modes and identifies leading candidate materials.
conclusion: Provides a comprehensive overview for researchers, highlighting open questions and future directions.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review connects statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to large-scale neural recordings, aiming to uncover reproducible collective behaviors in brain networks.
motivation: The authors aim to bridge theoretical statistical physics with quantitative neuroscience experiments to find universal principles in neural network activity.
method: The paper reviews recent work applying maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to multi-neuron recording data.
result: It highlights that these methods reveal reproducible, quantitative behaviors in neural networks, suggesting that abstract physical principles can have predictive power in neuroscience.
conclusion: The review argues for the value of statistical physics approaches in understanding brain function, but it is not directly aligned with the specified research directions.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on photophysical processes.
motivation: To understand and model nonradiative transitions in molecules and materials, relevant to photonics and energy harvesting.
method: Reviews various theoretical approaches for describing internal conversion, including quantum dynamics and rate theories.
result: Summarizes current methods and their applicability to applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
conclusion: Provides an outlook on incorporating these models into practical studies, but does not present new results.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their formation and quantum features.
motivation: To provide an overview of quantum-mechanical properties of skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics and quantum technologies.
method: A review article summarizing theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion quantum properties, including interactions and quantum dynamics.
result: The paper discusses quantum effects in skyrmion formation and the possibility of skyrmions exhibiting quantum behavior, but does not present new research findings.
conclusion: Skyrmions may offer a platform for studying quantum topological phenomena, but the paper is a review without novel contributions to the user's specific research directions.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, potentially mediated by new bosons and relevant to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To consolidate the state of the art in searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions, which could reveal new physics beyond the standard model and shed light on dark matter and dark energy.
method: The paper is a review that summarizes theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent exotic interactions and surveys experimental techniques used to search for them.
result: The review catalogs various theoretical models and experimental constraints, highlighting the current status and future prospects for detecting such interactions.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, with ongoing experimental efforts and theoretical developments.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining that apparent violations arise from violating assumptions in the bounds' derivation.
motivation: To clarify why some measured material properties exceed classical thermodynamic bounds and to show how designing materials to violate these assumptions can yield interesting properties.
method: The paper is a review (Colloquium) that surveys various circumstances where measurements exceed thermodynamic bounds and identifies which underlying assumptions are violated in each case.
result: It catalogs many examples of apparent violations and explains the assumptions behind them, also discussing how to engineer materials to exploit these effects.
conclusion: Apparent violations of thermodynamic bounds are not actual violations but result from misapplied assumptions; understanding this can guide the development of novel materials.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical approaches to simulating quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries such as fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology, potentially revealing new physics.
method: The paper surveys implementations in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems, discussing theoretical frameworks and experimental techniques for realizing these geometries.
result: It provides a comprehensive overview of current capabilities and challenges in simulating quantum matter in nonstandard geometries.
conclusion: The field is promising for advancing quantum simulation, but the paper is a review without novel technical contributions directly aligned with the specified research directions.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: This review explores self-alignment in active matter systems, where particles align their orientation with their velocity, leading to novel collective behaviors.
motivation: The paper aims to unify and understand the role of self-alignment in active matter, which is a key mechanism in biological and synthetic systems.
method: It provides a comprehensive review of existing models and experiments, introducing a unified mathematical and conceptual framework for self-alignment.
result: The review highlights how self-alignment leads to phenomena such as orbiting in traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, and discusses potential applications.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental property that reshapes active matter dynamics, offering new avenues for research and applications in biology, materials, and robotics.

title: Wrinkles, Creases, And Cusps In Growing Soft Matter
authors: Martine Ben Amar
abstract:
Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

The buckling of a material surface subject to compression or growth is a ubiquitous phenomenon, arising in materials science contexts such as the swelling of gels as well as in biological contexts such as morphogenesis and embryogenesis. A complete understanding of the creases and sharp cusps that commonly accompany buckling requires nonlinear elasticity theory. This review presents a modern treatment of the Biot instability, integrating many standard techniques of nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, such as bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015004] Published Mon Feb 24, 2025.
tldr: This review covers nonlinear elasticity theory for buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to provide a modern treatment of the Biot instability in soft matter, integrating nonlinear physics and solid mechanics techniques.
method: It reviews bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and integral methods applied to nonlinear elasticity.
result: The review synthesizes existing knowledge on crease and cusp formation in growing soft materials.
conclusion: The work is a contribution to soft matter physics and mechanics, not to the user's research directions.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: This review paper discusses experimental and theoretical efforts to probe gravity using massive quantum systems, focusing on decoherence and entanglement mediated by gravity.
motivation: The authors aim to review the current state of research on testing gravity's quantum effects using massive quantum systems, as classical gravity is poorly tested and quantum probes may reveal new physics.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical proposals and experimental state-of-the-art for studying gravity-induced decoherence and entanglement in massive quantum systems.
result: The review summarizes ongoing experiments and theoretical frameworks for detecting quantum gravitational effects, such as gravity-mediated entanglement and collapse models.
conclusion: The authors conclude that experiments testing quantum gravity effects are underway and will guide future theoretical descriptions of gravity at the quantum scale.

title: Topological Evolution Of Band Degeneracies And Bound States In The Continuum In Anisotropic Photonic Crystal Slabs
authors: Xin Gao, Ze-Huan Zheng, Qilin Duan, Huanyang Chen And Ying Chen
abstract: Topological degeneracies, such as Dirac or Weyl points and exceptional points, play a vital role in photonics and metamaterials due to their unique topological characteristics. This study investigates the intricate evolution of topological charges in degenerate bands, focusing on the interactions among bound states in the continuum (BICs), degenerate states (DS) and circularly polarized states (C points). Specifically, by controlling the optical axis (OA) orientation in anisotropic materials to break azimuthal anisotropy symmetry, we elucidate the evolutionary laws of DS and BICs in momentum space with the rotation of OA, and clarify the accompanying phenomena of charge annihilation and generation. When polar anisotropy symmetry is broken, the complex processes including splitting of BICs, migration of C points and the charge reversal of Γ-point BICs are further displayed. Our work introduces an additional degree of freedom for modulating band degeneracies and their associated topological properties, inspiring future developments in singularity physics through engineering naturally anisotropic materials.
tldr: This paper studies topological charges and bound states in the continuum in anisotropic photonic crystal slabs, focusing on band degeneracies and their evolution.
motivation: The authors aim to understand and control topological degeneracies in photonic systems, which are important for photonics applications.
method: They theoretically analyze the evolution of topological charges, bound states in the continuum (BICs), and circularly polarized states by varying the optical axis orientation in anisotropic materials.
result: They reveal how breaking azimuthal and polar anisotropy symmetries leads to charge annihilation, generation, splitting of BICs, and charge reversal at the Γ point.
conclusion: The work introduces a new degree of freedom for modulating band degeneracies and topological properties in photonic crystals, potentially inspiring future developments in singularity physics.

title: Visualizing The Effect Of Engineered Internal Perturbations On An Artificial 2d Atom And Explaining It Using Perturbation Theory
authors: Marco Weiss And Franz J Giessibl Fabian Stilp
abstract: Atomic orbitals are affected by external perturbations, such as the proximity of other atoms or exposure to electric or magnetic fields, that induce Stark and Zeemann splittings. The thought experiment: What would happen with these orbitals if one would position a fraction of a positive elementary charge with a tweezer at about half the atomic radius? This would allow for a highly controlled experiment on the alteration of atomic orbitals by a perturbation. Such a tweezer does not exist, so this remains a thought experiment. However, we can achieve something similar in an artificial 2D atom such as a quantum corral where we put single adsorbate atoms inside, which can be engineered by lateral manipulation with scanning probe microscopy. We show that the perturbation potential qualitatively follows the one between two natural atoms, a long-range attraction followed by a short-range repulsion. We demonstrate the state-selectivity of the short-range interaction leading to tunable electronic states. Surprisingly, long-range Coulomb attraction can be detected experimentally, even though charges are strongly screened on the metal surface. We estimate an effective charge of the adsorbate on the order of 1/1000 of an elementary charge. The perturbed orbital is imaged by atomic force microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy and described by perturbation theory. As a practical application, this introduces the ability to tune the geometry of the reactivity of an artificial atom, similar to the change in the chemical reactivity of a natural atom, when it is bound to other atoms.
tldr: This paper studies the effect of engineered internal perturbations on a 2D artificial atom (quantum corral) using scanning probe microscopy and perturbation theory.
motivation: To understand how atomic orbitals respond to perturbations by creating a controllable artificial atom, and to explore the possibility of tuning its electronic properties.
method: The authors use scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy to image the perturbed orbitals of a quantum corral with adsorbate atoms inside, and compare with perturbation theory calculations.
result: They observe state-selective short-range interactions and long-range Coulomb attraction, estimating an effective charge of the adsorbate on the order of 1/1000 of an elementary charge.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the ability to tune the geometry of reactivity of an artificial atom, analogous to chemical reactivity changes in natural atoms, but it is primarily an experimental surface science study.

title: Superluminal Transformations And Indeterminism
authors: Amrapali Sen And Flavio Del Santo
abstract: Quantum theory is widely regarded as fundamentally indeterministic, yet classical frameworks can also exhibit indeterminism once infinite information is abandoned. At the same time, relativity is usually taken to forbid superluminal signalling, although Lorentz symmetry formally admits superluminal transformations (SpTs). Dragan and Ekert have argued that SpTs entail a form of indeterminism analogous to that encountered in quantum theory. Here, we derive a theory-independent no-go theorem from a set of natural assumptions: any framework admitting non-order-preserving SpTs must either abandon finite information, relinquish time-symmetric informational content, deny that the past stores memory, or abandon the notion that time determines a preferred causal ordering. In particular, one possible implication is that any theory accommodating SpTs suggests an ontology with unbounded informational content, akin to deterministic classical theories formulated over the real numbers. Consequently, any ontic indeterminacy associated with superluminal transformations cannot originate from finite information.
tldr: This paper derives a no-go theorem for theories admitting superluminal transformations, linking them to indeterminism and infinite information, but it does not align with the specified research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to explore the implications of superluminal transformations for indeterminism, building on prior work by Dragan and Ekert, and to provide a theory-independent analysis.
method: They derive a no-go theorem from a set of natural assumptions about information, time symmetry, memory, and causal ordering, and analyze the consequences for ontic indeterminacy.
result: The theorem shows that any framework with non-order-preserving superluminal transformations must either abandon finite information, time-symmetric content, memory, or preferred causal ordering, implying unbounded informational content and no ontic indeterminacy from finite information.
conclusion: The paper suggests that superluminal transformations do not inherently lead to quantum-like indeterminism, and any such indeterminacy cannot arise from finite information constraints.

title: Searching For Quantum Effects In The Brain: A Bell-type Test For Nonclassical Latent Representations In Autoencoders
authors: Iannis K Kominis, Can Xie, Shuguang Li, Michael Skotiniotis And Giorgos P Tsironis
abstract: Whether neural information processing is entirely classical or involves quantum-mechanical elements remains an open question. Here we propose a model-agnostic, information-theoretic test of nonclassicality that bypasses microscopic assumptions and instead probes the structure of neural representations themselves. Using autoencoders as a transparent model system, we introduce a Bell-type consistency test in latent space, and ask whether decoding statistics obtained under multiple readout contexts can be jointly explained by a single positive latent-variable distribution. By shifting the search for quantum-like signatures in neural systems from microscopic dynamics to experimentally testable constraints on information processing, this work opens a new route for probing the fundamental physics of neural computation. The proposed test identifies violations of classical latent-variable consistency at the level of statistical representations, without assuming a specific underlying physical mechanism.
tldr: This paper proposes a Bell-type consistency test for latent representations in autoencoders to probe nonclassicality in neural information processing, but it is not aligned with the specified research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to detect quantum-like effects in neural systems without microscopic assumptions, using an information-theoretic approach.
method: They introduce a model-agnostic test in latent space, checking whether decoding statistics under multiple contexts can be explained by a single classical latent-variable distribution.
result: The test identifies violations of classical consistency, suggesting potential nonclassical signatures in neural representations.
conclusion: The work opens a new route for probing fundamental physics of neural computation, but it is not directly relevant to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: From Intuition To Optimization: A Review Of Inverse Design Applied To Optical Nanotweezers
authors: Sejeong Kim And Kenneth B Crozier Damian Nelson
abstract: Optical nanotweezers, which integrate nanophotonic structures such as plasmonic antennas, dielectric resonators, and metasurfaces, have emerged as powerful tools for manipulating nanoparticles, biomolecules, and viruses with high precision. However, traditional designs rely heavily on heuristic approaches and simple geometries, limiting performance. Inverse design offers a paradigm shift by using computational optimization methods to discover non-intuitive, high-performance structures for optical trapping. This review provides an overview of key inverse design methodologies, including adjoint-based optimization, topology optimization, and machine learning approaches, and highlights their broader impact across nanophotonics. We then focus on their application to optical nanotweezers, where recent advances demonstrate enhanced trapping stiffness, reduced optical heating, and tailored trapping landscapes. Representative examples include algorithmic design of plasmonic nanotweezers, topology-optimized plasmonic nanoapertures, inverse-designed dielectric nanocavities, and force-centric designs based on Maxwell stress tensor engineering. Collectively, these studies illustrate how inverse design enables stable, efficient, and versatile optical trapping at the nanoscale. Despite these advances, challenges remain in fabrication, computational cost, and the interpretability of optimized structures. We conclude with a perspective on future directions, emphasizing opportunities in reconfigurable tweezers, lab-on-a-chip integration, and quantum nanophotonics. By bridging photonic optimization with nanoscale manipulation, inverse-designed optical nanotweezers offer promising opportunities for future applications in biophysics, materials science, and quantum technologies.
tldr: A review of inverse design methods for optical nanotweezers, focusing on computational optimization for nanophotonic trapping.
motivation: Traditional optical tweezers rely on heuristic designs, limiting performance; inverse design offers a systematic optimization approach.
method: The paper reviews adjoint-based optimization, topology optimization, and machine learning approaches applied to optical nanotweezers.
result: Inverse design enhances trapping stiffness, reduces heating, and enables tailored trapping landscapes, with examples in plasmonic and dielectric structures.
conclusion: Inverse-designed optical nanotweezers show promise for biophysics and quantum technologies, but face challenges in fabrication and computational cost.

title: Review On Band Structure And Spin Polarization Of Altermagnetic Materials
authors: Xiangnan Xie, Xiaoyue He, Fayuan Zhang And Chaoyu Chen
abstract: Recent theoretical and experimental efforts have revealed the existence of a new class of magnetic materials, altermagnets, characterized by distinct symmetries in spin and real space. Combining the properties of ferromagnets, such as band spin polarization and time-reversal symmetry breaking responses, and antiferromagnets, like vanishing stray field and terahertz magnon dynamics, altermagnets are attracting enormous attention in both magnetism and spintronics community. While numerous altermagnetic candidates and emerging physical properties have been studied in theory extensively and enthusiastically, the experimental investigation of altermagnetism is struggling against the lack of proper altermagnetic materials and the controversial results reported for specific candidates. In this review, we first give a general description on the concept and key properties of altermagnetism, outline its distinction from other compensated magnetic order from the aspects of time-reversal symmetry in the spin momentum locking texture and time-reversal symmetry breaking responses. The main body of this review concentrates on the progress in altermagnetic material study with special focus on their band structure and spin polarization features, as well as the controversies over several candidate materials. Going forward, we point out several directions which altermagnetic material investigation might follow and guidelines which could help to avoid the pitfalls in the experimental pursuit of ideal altermagnets.
tldr: This review summarizes the band structure and spin polarization properties of altermagnetic materials, a new class of magnetic materials with combined ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic features.
motivation: Altermagnets are promising for spintronics, but experimental investigation is hindered by lack of suitable materials and controversial results. This review aims to consolidate theoretical and experimental progress and provide guidelines.
method: The authors review the concept of altermagnetism, distinguish it from other magnetic orders, and survey candidate materials with focus on band structure and spin polarization, highlighting controversies.
result: The review outlines key properties of altermagnets, discusses experimental challenges, and suggests future research directions and guidelines for identifying ideal altermagnets.
conclusion: Altermagnetic materials are an emerging field with potential for spintronics, but more experimental work is needed to confirm candidates and understand their properties.

title: Switchable Band Alignment In 2D-perovskite/WS2 Heterostructures For Tunable Exciton Transport And Valley Polarization
authors: Yingying Chen, Zeyi Liu, Zisheng Gong, Cheng Wang, Wendian Yao, Junze Li, Ti Wang, Weibo Gao And Dehui Li
abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures integrated by two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) hold great potential for engineering promising exciton phenomena, particularly interlayer excitons (IXs) featuring extended lifetimes and permanent out-of-plane electric dipole moments. While electrically controllable IX emission has been extensively explored in TMD heterobilayers, reconfiguring their band alignment to achieve selected exciton states and exploit these states for novel excitonic functionalities remains an urgent challenge. Here, we demonstrate dynamic exciton control by electrically tunable band alignment transitions between type-II and type-I configurations in WS2/(iso-BA)2PbI4 heterostructures, enabling reversible conversion between charged interlayer (IX±) and charged intralayer (X−) excitons. By tailoring these exciton states, we achieve two critical functionalities: (i) 7 μm ON/OFF control of exciton transport via transition between delocalized IX± (ON) and confined X− (OFF) states; (ii) valley polarization switching with a 16.3 ON/OFF ratio, leveraging distinct spin-valley configurations of IX± (unpolarized) and X− (polarized). Unlike twist-angle-dependent TMD heterobilayers, this platform operates independently of stacking alignment, establishing a broadly hybrid 2D system as a practical paradigm towards programmable nanophotonic circuits.
tldr: This paper demonstrates electrically tunable band alignment transitions in WS2/perovskite heterostructures to control exciton transport and valley polarization.
motivation: The authors aim to achieve dynamic control of exciton states in van der Waals heterostructures, enabling novel excitonic functionalities for nanophotonic circuits.
method: They fabricate WS2/(iso-BA)2PbI4 heterostructures and apply electric fields to switch between type-II and type-I band alignments, converting between charged interlayer and intralayer excitons.
result: They achieve 7 μm ON/OFF control of exciton transport and valley polarization switching with a 16.3 ON/OFF ratio.
conclusion: This platform offers a twist-angle-independent approach for programmable exciton control, potentially useful for nanophotonic devices.

title: Exploring Exotic Spin-dependent Interactions Beyond The Standard Model: Theoretical Foundations And Experimental Investigations
authors: L Y Wu And H Yan
abstract: New interactions mediated by novel particles propose solutions to several important questions in modern physics. Axions serve as examples of such particles; they are lightweight and interact weakly with ordinary matter. This category of particles, including those similar to axions—termed axion-like particles (ALPs)—arises from diverse theoretical frameworks, such as the Peccei-Quinn mechanism addressing the strong CP problem, string theory, and spontaneous supersymmetry breaking. Given their light mass and weak coupling, ALPs are also possible candidates for cold dark matter. Introducing these new interactions mediated by novel particles not only tackles several challenges in modern physics but also raises a crucial question: Are there undiscovered interactions beyond the standard model (SM)? Many of the interactions predicted by these theories are spin-dependent, which is the primary focus of this review. In this review, we first outline the theoretical foundations for investigating exotic spin-dependent interactions, highlighting their importance in various models beyond the SM. We examine the potential roles of new lightweight particles in mediating these interactions, which may enhance our understanding of dark matter. Relevant formulas derived from theoretical models are included to support experimental investigations. Following this theoretical framework, we conduct a detailed review of recent experimental efforts to detect these exotic interactions. A systematic review of current constraints on these interactions is presented, along with an assessment of various detection approaches.
tldr: A review of theoretical and experimental searches for exotic spin-dependent interactions mediated by axion-like particles, motivated by physics beyond the Standard Model.
motivation: To explore potential new forces beyond the Standard Model, particularly spin-dependent interactions mediated by light particles like axions, which may also address dark matter.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks (e.g., Peccei-Quinn, string theory) and derives relevant formulas, then surveys experimental techniques and constraints from various detection approaches.
result: It provides a systematic compilation of current experimental constraints on exotic spin-dependent interactions and assesses different detection methods.
conclusion: The review highlights the ongoing search for new physics but does not present novel results; it serves as a reference for the field.

title: Non-spreading Meronic Spin Defects Around Optical Vortices
authors: Miguel A Porras And Yijie Shen Nilo Mata-Cervera
abstract: Optical vortices are singularity lines where the light field intensity vanishes and its phase is undefined. These threads of darkness are adorned by Gauss’s law as lines of pure longitudinal polarization where the polarization plane tilts and winds around. The resulting spin field is as a unique structure with both features of topological texture and defect, as it includes a point defect of undefined spin enclosed by a meronic texture which spans half the spin unit sphere. This topological structure does not spread in propagation: the normalized spin field maintains a deep-subwavelength confinement around the vortex line while the underlying vortex beam continues to diffract. From their intrinsic nature and subwavelength confinement, these textures exhibit enhanced robustness upon isotropic perturbations such as atmospheric turbulence compared with other tailored polarization textures. Here we describe these topologies of transverse spin which decorate the phase singularity of paraxial vortex beams, highlighting the diversity of topological structures that arise in two different spaces—the spin unit sphere and the transverse-axial Poincaré sphere—and discuss the underlying aspects behind their subwavelength localization.
tldr: This paper describes topological spin textures (meronic defects) around optical vortices, focusing on their subwavelength confinement and robustness to perturbations.
motivation: To understand and characterize the topological structures of transverse spin that decorate phase singularities in paraxial vortex beams, and to highlight their potential for robust optical applications.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the spin field around optical vortices, using concepts from topology and Poincaré sphere representations, and discuss the underlying physics of subwavelength localization.
result: They find that the normalized spin field forms a meronic texture with a point defect, which remains deeply subwavelength confined during propagation and shows enhanced robustness to isotropic perturbations like atmospheric turbulence.
conclusion: These non-spreading meronic spin defects represent a novel class of topological structures in optics with potential for robust applications, but the work is primarily theoretical and not directly connected to quantum information or quantum thermodynamics.

title: Observation Of Floquet Tensor Monopoles
authors: Hao Yuan, Weixuan Zhang, Na Sun And Xiangdong Zhang
abstract: Tensor monopoles, topological singularities of Kalb–Ramond tensor gauge fields, have garnered widespread attention in high-energy and condensed matter physics. They give rise to exotic phenomena such as quantized magnetoelectric responses and chiral boundary states, acting as potential building blocks for the development of topological devices in high-dimensional space. However, theoretical studies and experimental realizations reported to date have remained in static settings, and the realization of Floquet tensor monopoles (FTMs) and their associated anomalous non-equilibrium topological features has yet to be achieved. Here, we report the first theoretical and experimental implementation of FTMs in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system. We systematically uncover the driving-frequency controlled creation, motion, and annihilation of FTMs, together with their anomalous bulk-edge correspondence. These phenomena are unique to FTMs and have no static counterparts. In experiments, we design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits, and directly observe the controllable motion of FTMs in k-space and their induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states by tuning the driving frequency. Our findings extend tensor monopole research to the non-equilibrium regime, providing a theoretical and experimental platform for exploring exotic topological phases in dynamic tensor gauge fields and laying the groundwork for functional topological devices with real-time control.
tldr: This paper reports the first experimental realization of Floquet tensor monopoles in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system using time-varying topological circuits.
motivation: Tensor monopoles have been studied in static settings, but their non-equilibrium (Floquet) counterparts and associated anomalous topological features have not been realized.
method: The authors design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits to implement a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system, and tune the driving frequency to control the creation, motion, and annihilation of Floquet tensor monopoles.
result: They directly observe the controllable motion of Floquet tensor monopoles in k-space and the induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states, demonstrating anomalous bulk-edge correspondence unique to Floquet tensor monopoles.
conclusion: This work extends tensor monopole research to the non-equilibrium regime, providing a platform for exploring dynamic tensor gauge fields and functional topological devices with real-time control.

title: Excitonic Energy Transfer In Red Algal Photosystem I Reveals An Evolutionary Bridge Between Cyanobacteria And Plants
authors: Mengyuan Cuizihui Liumiriam Izzojunhua Zhouenhu Hevandana Tiwaripetar H. Lambrevr. J. abstract:

SignificancePhotosystem I (PSI) converts sunlight into chemical energy with remarkable efficiency, yet how its energy-transfer pathways evolved across cyanobacteria, alga, and plants remain unclear. Using ultralow-temperature two-dimensional electronic ...
tldr: This paper studies excitonic energy transfer in red algal Photosystem I using two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy, revealing evolutionary links between cyanobacteria and plants.
motivation: To understand how energy-transfer pathways in Photosystem I evolved across different organisms, which is key to photosynthesis efficiency.
method: Ultralow-temperature two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy was used to probe excitonic energy transfer dynamics in red algal PSI.
result: The study reveals distinct energy-transfer pathways that bridge cyanobacterial and plant PSI, providing evolutionary insights.
conclusion: The findings clarify the evolution of photosynthetic energy transfer, but the work is primarily biological and not directly related to quantum information or quantum thermodynamics.

title: New Techniques For High-resolution Imaging And High-precision Wavefront Sensing Via Masked-aperture Interferometry
authors: Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, Bojan Nikolic, Chris Carilli, Laura Torino, Ubaldo Iriso
abstract: ArXiv:2607.27347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving high-angular-resolution imaging on subarcsecond scales is fundamentally limited by wavefront aberrations imparted by the propagation medium and by optical elements along the light path. Accurate recovery of source structure at these fine angular scales therefore relies on precise, real-time sensing and correction of wavefront aberrations. Drawing inspiration from radio interferometry, we have developed different approaches using masked apertures that directly measure both the amplitude and phase of the distortions to the electromagnetic wavefront while simultaneously reconstructing the underlying source structure. First is radio interferometry style self-calibration which can recover the complex electric field aberrations across the aperture with subarcsecond phase accuracy, equivalent to nanometer-level precision in optical pathlength, and simultaneously reconstruct the source structure with milliarcsecond (sub-micron) accuracy. Second is closure invariant-based source reconstruction which allows to bypass self-calibration and errors therein entirely while achieving comparable fidelity in the recovered source structure. These methods have been validated on the ALBA synchrotron beamline. Together, these methods provide a reliable framework for nanometre-scale high-precision wavefront sensing and subarcsecond-scale high angular resolution imaging, enabling new possibilities for masked-aperture interferometry. Potential applications span laboratory and synchrotron facilities to astronomy, including beam diagnostics in the Large Hadron Collider and masked-aperture interferometry on space telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope.
tldr: This paper presents new techniques for high-resolution imaging and wavefront sensing using masked-aperture interferometry, validated on a synchrotron beamline.
motivation: To overcome wavefront aberrations that limit subarcsecond imaging, the authors aim to develop methods that simultaneously sense wavefront errors and reconstruct source structure.
method: They adapt radio interferometry techniques, including self-calibration and closure invariants, to masked-aperture interferometry, measuring amplitude and phase distortions.
result: The methods achieve nanometer-level wavefront sensing precision and milliarcsecond imaging accuracy, validated on the ALBA synchrotron beamline.
conclusion: The framework enables high-precision wavefront sensing and high-resolution imaging, with potential applications in astronomy and beam diagnostics.

title: Vector Field Theory In Motion: Revealing Latent Potentials In Soccer Dynamics
authors: Paula Rodr\'iguez-S\'anchez, Roberto L\'opez Del Campo, Ricardo Resta, Jos\'e J. Ramasco, Javier M. Buld\'u, Johann H. Mart\'inez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.27838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Team sports offer a natural laboratory for studying collective motion in competitive environments. While recent tracking technologies enabled detailed analysis of player and ball trajectories, most existing approaches rely on discrete events and local kinematic descriptors. This limits the possibility of studying team collective behavior. Here we introduce a physics-based framework to characterize collective dynamics using empirically reconstructed velocity vector fields defined over the pitch. Taking soccer as a paradigmatic example, we show that both ball and player movements generate smooth, predominantly irrotational vector fields. Each of these fields is generated by a potential providing compact, physically interpretable representations of collective motion and encoding how teams control, or constrain play across space during attacking and defensive phases in each match. Applied to an entire season of top-level competition, the resulting potentials reveal stable team-specific fingerprints and quantitative associations between potential gradients and effective ball progression.
tldr: This paper applies physics-based vector field analysis to soccer dynamics, revealing latent potentials that characterize team collective motion.
motivation: Existing sports analytics rely on discrete events and local kinematics, limiting the study of collective team behavior. The authors aim to provide a compact, physically interpretable representation of team dynamics.
method: They reconstruct velocity vector fields from player and ball trajectories, show they are predominantly irrotational, and derive scalar potentials. They analyze an entire season of top-level soccer to extract team-specific fingerprints and relate potential gradients to ball progression.
result: The potentials reveal stable team-specific patterns and quantitative associations between potential gradients and effective ball progression.
conclusion: The framework offers a novel way to characterize collective motion in team sports, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Dynamical Low-Rank Filters For Data Assimilation
authors: Yoshihito Kazashi, Youssef Marzouk, Fabio Nobile, Fabio Zoccolan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.27432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose dynamical low-rank (DLR) type filters for data-assimilation problems based on stochastic differential equations (SDEs). In detail, first we derive a DLRA filter for minimizing jointly the mean and covariance error, as well as a strategy to efficiently include the relevant orthogonal directions. This last approach allows the main subspace to evolve also according to the observation operator. Those procedures naturally extend to a Kalman-Bucy type filter when dealing with linear drift, and to ensemble methods, too, resulting also suitable for problems described by nonlinear drift and possible non-Gaussian distribution. Moreover, we further propose a preliminary particle-type DLRA filter that shows potentiality in nonlinear settings. Numerical simulations show the efficacy of these procedures in relevant applications, opening up to further studies in these filtering directions.
tldr: This paper proposes dynamical low-rank filters for data assimilation in stochastic differential equations, focusing on computational efficiency for high-dimensional state estimation.
motivation: Data assimilation in high-dimensional systems is computationally challenging; low-rank approximations can reduce cost while maintaining accuracy.
method: The authors derive dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) filters that minimize mean and covariance error, incorporate observation directions, and extend to Kalman-Bucy and ensemble methods, plus a particle-type filter.
result: Numerical simulations demonstrate efficacy in relevant applications, showing improved performance and scalability.
conclusion: The proposed filters offer promising tools for data assimilation, opening avenues for further research in filtering and uncertainty quantification.

title: Adaptive Security At The Edge For 6G-Enabled Healthcare IoT
authors: Ijaz Ahmad, Ijaz Ahmad, Erkki Harjula
abstract: ArXiv:2607.27858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Healthcare IoT services increasingly rely on edge gateways to relay routine telemetry and deliver rare but timecritical alarms. Even short traffic bursts can inflate worstcase delay and interfere with urgent messages. We present NANOEDGEGUARD, a kernel-plane closed-loop controller that observes per-source traffic intensity at the edge and enforces an auditable, multi-tier rate policy using in-kernel traffic-control hooks. Unlike static firewall rules or user-space control loops, our design prioritizes fast actuation and explicit recovery through hysteresis, and it records policy transitions for auditability. Using a Raspberry Pi gateway hosting an MQTT broker and two ESP32 endpoints generating vitals, alarms, and a timed burst, we show that adaptive kernel-plane rate control reduces the 99th-percentile alarm RTT by 13.3% compared to a user-space firewall baseline while maintaining no-enforcement-level RTT, and it reduces excess admitted burst traffic by 46% compared to no enforcement. These early results indicate that adaptive, auditable enforcement at the gateway can improve resilience for healthcare IoT, and it can be extended toward on-demand policy deployment in future edge intelligence.
tldr: This paper presents a kernel-plane adaptive rate control system for healthcare IoT edge gateways, focusing on network traffic management rather than quantum information.
motivation: Healthcare IoT edge gateways need to handle traffic bursts to ensure timely delivery of critical alarms, but static rules and user-space controls are insufficient.
method: The authors implement NANOEDGEGUARD, a closed-loop controller in the kernel plane that monitors per-source traffic and enforces multi-tier rate policies with hysteresis, using Linux traffic-control hooks.
result: Experiments on a Raspberry Pi gateway with MQTT and ESP32 endpoints show a 13.3% reduction in 99th-percentile alarm RTT and a 46% reduction in excess burst traffic compared to baselines.
conclusion: Adaptive kernel-plane enforcement improves resilience for healthcare IoT and can be extended for on-demand policy deployment in edge intelligence.

title: Security Of World-Model-Based Embodied Ai: A Lifecycle Of Threats, Defenses, And Evaluation
authors: Fazhong Liu, Zhuoyan Chen, Haozhen Tan, Yan Meng, Guoxing Chen, Haojin Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.28226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models give embodied AI a predictive core: they compress observations into states, simulate action-conditioned futures, and enable planning beyond reactive control. This predictive layer, however, opens a new security boundary-compromise can propagate from data, sensors, prompts, or feedback into physical action. Rather than treating world models as an isolated component, this survey traces threats across their entire lifecycle-from data construction and representation learning, through state grounding and imagination, to trajectory evaluation, execution, and long-term adaptation via memory and tools. We show that familiar attack families: poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection, trajectory manipulation, and supply-chain attacks take on distinct meanings when they corrupt world states, learned dynamics, affordance estimates, or safety costs. We also highlight a duality: world models can serve as runtime safety shields, yet when compromised or over-trusted they generate predictive safety illusions. The survey offers a lifecycle taxonomy, maps existing attacks to world-model security properties, outlines evaluation protocols for safety failures, and structures defenses across provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance.
tldr: A survey on security threats and defenses for world-model-based embodied AI, covering the full lifecycle from data to deployment.
motivation: World models in embodied AI introduce new security vulnerabilities that can propagate to physical actions, yet no comprehensive framework exists.
method: The paper proposes a lifecycle taxonomy, maps attack families to world-model components, and outlines defenses and evaluation protocols.
result: Identifies distinct security implications for world states, dynamics, affordances, and safety costs, and highlights the duality of world models as safety shields or sources of illusions.
conclusion: Calls for a lifecycle-aware security approach and structured defenses to mitigate risks in embodied AI systems.

title: Breaking Scale Separation In Metamaterials' Homogenization: Interface-Inertia-Enhanced Relaxed Micromorphic Model
authors: Angela Madeo, Leonardo Perez, Mohammad Sarhil
abstract: ArXiv:2607.27385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Homogenized continuum models are widely used to describe wave propagation and band-gap behavior in mechanical metamaterials without explicitly resolving their microstructure. Their validity, however, typically relies on the classical separation of scales assumption, according to which the wavelength of the propagating disturbance is much larger than the characteristic size of the unit cell. In finite-size metamaterial samples and at higher frequencies, this assumption progressively breaks down, and the dynamic response becomes strongly influenced by the way the microstructure is truncated at the external boundaries. In this work we introduce a fundamentally new concept in the homogenized description of mechanical metamaterials: the inertial contribution of macroscopic interfaces. We show that different truncations of the same lattice generate boundaries with distinct mass distributions, which lead to measurable differences in the dynamic response of finite-sized specimens. To capture this complex mechanism in a homogenized framework, we extend the relaxed micromorphic model by introducing a kinetic surface energy defined on the boundary of the considered body. This generates an additional inertial term in the boundary conditions that can be seen as the homogenized counterpart of the interface inertia produced by the truncation of the microstructure. As a result, the homogenized model can now distinguish between finite-sized specimens that share identical bulk properties but differ only in the configuration of their interfaces. The proposed formulation preserves the variational structure of the relaxed micromorphic model while enabling the continuum to reproduce boundary-dependent responses observed in fully resolved simulations, particularly in frequency regimes ....... See the PDF for the full abstract.
tldr: This paper introduces a relaxed micromorphic model with interface inertia to capture boundary effects in metamaterial homogenization, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The authors aim to address the breakdown of scale separation in metamaterial homogenization, where finite-size effects and boundary truncations affect dynamic response.
method: They extend the relaxed micromorphic model by adding a kinetic surface energy on boundaries, introducing an inertial term in boundary conditions to represent interface inertia from microstructure truncation.
result: The enhanced model can distinguish finite specimens with identical bulk properties but different interface configurations, reproducing boundary-dependent responses in frequency regimes where classical homogenization fails.
conclusion: The proposed formulation preserves variational structure while capturing interface inertia effects, offering a more accurate homogenized description for finite metamaterial samples.

title: Comparison Of A Parametric Physics-Informed Neural Network And A Tensorial Reduced-Order Model For The Shallow-Water Dam-Break Problem
authors: Anton Myshak, Md Rezwan Bin Mizan, Ilya Timofeyev
abstract: ArXiv:2607.27433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop two parametric data-driven reduced models: a physics-informed neural network (PINN) and a non-intrusive tensorial reduced-order model (TROM), and apply both approaches to the parametrized one-dimensional shallow-water dam-break problem.
